A: A 1930s house in Madison using mixed natural materials and open living spaces.
B: Its significance is a domestic design experiment in affordability and spatial efficiency, not simply the prestige of Wright’s name. That distinguishes it from a bespoke landscape retreat. Likely discovery leads include Taliesin, organic architecture, American craft, Japanese design, and Wright’s books; these are predictable leads to verify, not evidence of a buyer audience.

A: A 1930s Pennsylvania retreat with sandstone, glass and concrete terraces above a stream.
B: The central appeal is an unusually direct spatial relationship to landscape and water. Unlike Jacobs I, its commission was a bespoke retreat rather than an affordable-house prototype. Site experience and conservation are stronger explanations than a generic luxury label. Predictable cultural leads include Taliesin, the Guggenheim, MoMA, Japanese landscape aesthetics and other Wright sites.

A: A 1951 Illinois riverside retreat with an elevated steel structure and extensive glazing.
B: Radical visual continuity and structural reduction explain its importance; extensive glass and a floodplain also complicate everyday occupation. Likely associations include Bauhaus, Knoll, the Barcelona Pavilion, and minimalist art. These obvious modernist relationships are already available without an affinity API.

A: A 1949 California residence and studio using industrial components in a hillside setting.
B: Standardized construction and a densely personal collection of objects coexist here. Its appeal is warmer and more experimental than a generic steel-and-glass minimalism label suggests. Herman Miller, Vitra, MoMA, Powers of Ten, film/photography and Case Study architecture are predictable leads. A recommendation of those names alone adds little.

A: A 1908 Pasadena house with detailed woodwork, art glass and coordinated furnishings.
B: Integrated craft and the relationship between building and furniture explain its appeal better than a size comparison. Likely links include Stickley, Arts and Crafts collections, woodworking and Japanese-influenced design. The Huntington is an obvious research institution given its Greene and Greene material. These are thematic hypotheses, not a premium estimate.

A: A mid-19th-century Washington house enlarged to 21 rooms.
B: Its significance principally follows Douglass’s life, writing and political history rather than a canonical architect. Literature, abolitionist history and African American history institutions are predictable connections. The distinction matters: a cultural history visitor is not thereby a buyer of this architectural style. No demographic or demand inference follows.

A: A 2015 Garland house of 1,594 square feet, two floors, three bedrooms and 2.5 baths, with documented efficient construction.
B: Verified energy performance and practical domestic use are the supported differentiators. Building science, efficient appliances and sustainable construction are reasonable discovery themes; a famous-designer or collector narrative would be invented. The control tests whether Qloo can represent a home without relying on a museum or famous author.
